title: Parent-Teacher Meetings
objectives: Understand the purpose and format of parent-teacher meetings and conferences
Use reported speech accurately to convey what teachers and school staff have said
Ask and respond to questions about a child's academic progress using appropriate formal language
Write a summary of a parent-teacher meeting using reported speech and formal vocabulary

reading_passage.title: Making the Most of Parent-Teacher Conferences
reading_passage.text:
Parent-teacher conferences are a vital opportunity for families and educators to discuss a child's academic progress, social development, and any concerns that may have arisen during the school year. Despite their importance, many parents — particularly those from immigrant communities — feel anxious about attending, often because of language barriers or uncertainty about what to expect.

Teachers typically report on a student's performance across all subjects, highlighting both strengths and areas for improvement. They may tell parents that their child is excelling in reading but struggling with mathematics, or that the student has excellent attendance but needs to participate more actively in class discussions. These observations are meant to be constructive, not critical.

Experts advise parents to come prepared with questions. For instance, a parent might ask what specific support is available for a child who is finding a subject difficult, or how they can help at home with homework and revision. Teachers generally appreciate parents who engage actively in these conversations.

School counsellors note that communication between home and school is one of the strongest predictors of a child's academic success. Research shows that students whose parents attend meetings and maintain regular contact with teachers tend to perform better, feel more motivated, and develop stronger study habits than those whose parents have less involvement.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from the National Education Association Parent Engagement Handbook

glossary.meaning: a formal meeting to discuss a specific topic
performing extremely well; achieving at a high level
intended to be helpful and produce improvement, not to criticise
the process of reviewing and studying material already learned
something that indicates what is likely to happen in the future

comprehension.question: What two aspects of a child's development do teachers typically report on during a parent-teacher conference?
comprehension.answer: Teachers typically report on a student's academic progress and their social development.

comprehension.question: Why do you think the author specifically mentions immigrant communities when discussing anxiety about parent-teacher meetings?
comprehension.answer: Because immigrant parents may face additional challenges such as language barriers and unfamiliarity with the local education system, making parent-teacher meetings feel more daunting for them than for parents who grew up in the same country.

comprehension.question: The passage describes teachers' observations as 'constructive, not critical'. What is the difference between these two words in this context?
comprehension.answer: Constructive means the feedback is intended to help the child improve, while critical suggests negative judgement. The author is reassuring parents that teachers aim to support rather than judge their children.

comprehension.question: What conclusion can you draw from the final paragraph about the relationship between parental involvement and a child's academic success?
comprehension.answer: There is a strong positive relationship between parental involvement and academic outcomes. Children whose parents are actively involved in their education tend to perform better and develop stronger study habits, suggesting that what happens at home is just as important as what happens at school.

language_focus.title: Reported Speech
language_focus.explanation: Reported speech (also called indirect speech) is used to tell someone what another person said, without using their exact words. When reporting speech, the tense usually shifts back: present simple becomes past simple; past simple becomes past perfect; 'will' becomes 'would'. Pronouns and time expressions also change to reflect the new speaker's perspective. Reporting verbs include: said, told, explained, advised, mentioned, warned, and suggested.

examples.sentence: Direct: 'Your daughter is excelling in reading.' → Reported: The teacher said that my daughter was excelling in reading.
examples.note: Present simple ('is') shifts to past simple ('was') in reported speech. The pronoun also changes from 'your' to 'my'.

examples.sentence: Direct: 'You should help your child with revision at home.' → Reported: The teacher advised me to help my child with revision at home.
examples.note: After 'advise', use the infinitive structure: 'advised + object + to + verb', not a 'that' clause.

practice.sentence: Direct speech: 'Ahmed needs to participate more in class discussions.' Report what the teacher said using 'told'.
practice.answer: The teacher told me that Ahmed needed to participate more in class discussions.

practice.sentence: Direct speech: 'I will arrange extra support for your son.' Report what the teacher said using 'said'.
practice.answer: The teacher said that she would arrange extra support for my son.

practice.sentence: Direct speech: 'Come to see me if you have any concerns.' Report what the teacher said using 'advised'.
practice.answer: The teacher advised me to come to see her if I had any concerns.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: absolutely necessary or essential for something to succeed
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Parent-teacher conferences are a vital opportunity for families and educators to discuss a child's academic progress.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: (past participle of 'arise') emerged or come to exist as a problem or situation
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Parent-teacher conferences allow families and educators to discuss any concerns that may have arisen during the school year.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: to continue doing something over a period of time; to keep something at the same level
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Students whose parents attend meetings and maintain regular contact with teachers tend to perform better.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: the degree to which someone is involved and interested in an activity or situation
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Teachers generally appreciate parents who engage actively in these conversations.

speaking_task.context: You recently attended a parent-teacher meeting for your child. A friend who was unable to attend their own child's meeting asks you about your experience and what the teacher said.
speaking_task.prompt: Tell your friend what happened at the meeting. Report what the teacher said about your child's progress — including one positive point and one area for improvement. Also report any advice the teacher gave you. Use reported speech throughout your response.
useful_language: She said that my child was...
speaking_task.model_answer: It went well overall. The teacher told me that my son was making good progress in science and that he had a strong understanding of the topics covered this term. However, she also said that he needed to improve his written work, because his ideas were good but his paragraphs were not always clearly organised. She advised me to encourage him to plan his writing before he starts, and she mentioned that the school offered a homework club on Thursdays which she thought would be helpful for him.

writing_workshop.model_text: After attending the parent-teacher conference, I sat down and wrote a summary of what had been discussed. The teacher explained that my daughter was performing well in most subjects but said that she was finding mathematics challenging. She told me that my daughter often understood concepts in class but struggled to apply them independently during tests. The teacher advised me to practise multiplication and division with her at home and suggested that we use online maths games to make revision more enjoyable.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: This summary is effective because it uses a variety of reporting verbs (explained, said, told, advised, suggested) and correctly shifts tenses from present to past when converting direct speech to reported speech.
writing_workshop.task: Write a 100-150 word summary of an imaginary parent-teacher meeting. Include what the teacher said about the child's strengths, what area needed improvement, and what advice was given. Use at least four different reporting verbs and apply tense shifts correctly throughout.
success_criteria: Uses at least four different reporting verbs (e.g. said, told, explained, advised, warned, mentioned, suggested)
Correctly shifts verb tenses from direct speech into reported speech
Covers at least three points: a strength, an area for improvement, and a piece of advice

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly converts this direct speech into reported speech? Direct: 'Your son is doing very well in history.'
options: The teacher said that my son is doing very well in history.
The teacher said that my son was doing very well in history.
The teacher told that my son was doing very well in history.
The teacher said my son does very well in history.
quiz.explanation: In reported speech, the present tense ('is doing') shifts to past tense ('was doing'). 'Said that' is also the correct structure — 'told that' without an object is incorrect.

quiz.question: Which reporting verb is followed by 'object + to + infinitive'?
quiz.explanation: 'Advised' is followed by 'object + to + infinitive': 'She advised me to help my child.' 'Said', 'mentioned', and 'explained' are followed by 'that + clause'.

quiz.question: According to the passage, what is described as one of the strongest predictors of a child's academic success?
options: Having a large number of school subjects
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'School counsellors note that communication between home and school is one of the strongest predictors of a child's academic success.'

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly reports: 'We will hold another meeting next month'?
options: She said they will hold another meeting next month.
She said they would hold another meeting the following month.
She told they would hold another meeting next month.
She said they held another meeting the following month.
quiz.explanation: 'Will' becomes 'would' in reported speech. 'Next month' becomes 'the following month' because time expressions change when reporting from a different time/place. 'She said' (not 'she told') is used without an indirect object.

listening_exercises.transcript: Thank you for coming in, Mrs. Hassan. Overall, Ayan is doing very well. Her reading has improved a lot this semester, and she works hard in class. In math she sometimes needs extra time, so I'm sending home practice sheets twice a week. She's also very kind to other students. Do you have any questions about how you can support her at home?
listening_exercises.question: What does the teacher say about Ayan's reading?

listening_exercises.transcript: Parent-teacher conferences are usually short — about fifteen minutes — so come prepared. Write your questions before you go. Good questions include: How is my child doing compared to grade level? What can we practice at home? How is my child doing socially? If you need an interpreter, tell the school in advance — schools must provide one for free. Your questions show the teacher you care.
listening_exercises.question: What should parents do if they need an interpreter?
options: Pay for one at the meeting
